title: Distributed Data Access
subtitle: Reach another domain without erasing its boundary
summary: A service often needs data owned by another service, but direct table access breaks bounded contexts and makes change control harder. The chapter presents four patterns. Inter-service communication preserves ownership through a request contract, yet adds network latency, dependency, and aggregation work. Column schema replication copies selected fields into a consumer schema, improving local performance and availability while creating synchronization and ownership problems. Replicated caching keeps data in each service’s memory, giving fast access and independent scaling for relatively small, stable data; its costs include initial startup dependency, memory multiplication, configuration complexity, and poor fit for large or volatile data. A shared data domain puts tables in one schema, preserving SQL joins, constraints, consistency, and speed, but broadens change and security boundaries. The choice depends on volume, update rate, latency, availability, consistency, and the number of service instances. The Sysops Squad example selects replicated caching for small, mostly static expert profiles.

concepts.title: Inter-service calls
concepts.body: A service can request data through the owning service’s API and receive a contract that hides storage details. Ownership stays clear and data need not be synchronized, but each request adds network latency and a runtime availability dependency. Aggregating many calls can hurt responsiveness, throughput, and fault tolerance, especially when the owner is unavailable.
concepts.example: Wishlist asks Catalog for product descriptions. The API protects Catalog’s schema, but a product page now needs a timeout, retry policy, and behavior when Catalog cannot answer.

concepts.title: Column replication
concepts.body: Column schema replication copies only the fields a consumer needs into another table or schema. Reads become local and independent, avoiding repeated network calls and improving performance. The copied value can become stale, synchronization must be built and monitored, and the consumer may gain an implicit write or ownership concern. This pattern suits selected, manageable fields where eventual freshness is acceptable.
concepts.example: Wishlist stores product name and thumbnail copied from Catalog. Catalog remains the writer; an update stream refreshes replicas and reports lag when a consumer misses an event.

concepts.title: Replicated cache
concepts.body: Replicated caching keeps an owner’s data in synchronized in-memory copies inside each dependent service. It offers very fast reads, fault tolerance after initial population, and independent scale. It is a poor fit for large or rapidly changing data because memory multiplies per instance and propagation can lag. The first dependent instance also waits for the owner or another populated peer during startup.
concepts.example: Ticket Assignment caches 900 mostly static expert profiles. With two User Management and four Ticket Assignment instances, the team checks total memory and startup ordering before adopting the pattern.

concepts.title: Shared data domain
concepts.body: A shared schema lets services join tables directly and retain foreign keys, views, triggers, and stored procedures. It avoids network dependencies, replication, and synchronization, and gives excellent consistency and query performance. The cost is a broader bounded context: table changes may affect several services, governance and security become harder, and ownership is less isolated.
concepts.example: Wishlist and Product tables share a schema, so a SQL join returns descriptions immediately. A column change in either table may now require coordinated consumers and tighter access controls.

misconceptions.claim: A distributed cache is equivalent to replicated in-memory caching.
misconceptions.correction: A centralized distributed cache remains a remote dependency and can blur ownership. Replicated caching keeps synchronized copies inside services and removes the external cache hop.

misconceptions.claim: Local copies are always safer than an API call.
misconceptions.correction: Copies trade runtime dependency for synchronization, memory, startup, and freshness costs. The right pattern depends on volume, volatility, and consistency requirements.

scenario.title: Serve expert profiles
scenario.context: Ticket Assignment needs skill, zones, and scheduled availability from User Management. The data is 1.2 MB total, relatively static, and must be read quickly. Ticket Assignment may run four instances; User Management may run two. The services are separate domains and the assignment path cannot tolerate repeated network latency.

options.label: Replicate cache
options.benefit: Reads are local and fast, and assignment keeps running after the owner is temporarily unavailable once populated.
options.cost: Memory multiplies across instances and the first instance depends on owner startup and cache-product configuration.
options.consequence: User Management owns writes and populates a read-only replica. The team measures memory, startup sequencing, update lag, and product licensing before rollout.

options.label: Service calls
options.benefit: No duplicate memory or synchronization stream; User Management remains the sole source.
options.cost: Every assignment depends on network latency and User Management availability.
options.consequence: Ticket Assignment requests profiles with timeouts and retries. During owner outages assignment slows or pauses, but profile freshness and deployment setup remain simple.

scenario.debrief: Small, static data and strict latency favor replicated caching, provided startup and memory costs are acceptable. Volatile or large data would shift the balance toward calls or another pattern.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of inter-service communication?
options: It preserves ownership behind a contract
It enables foreign keys across databases
quiz.explanation: The owner controls storage and exposes a contract. The call still introduces latency and dependency.

quiz.question: Which data most suits replicated caching?
options: A small, mostly static reference dataset
A table requiring cross-service ACID writes
quiz.explanation: Replicas multiply memory and propagate updates, so small and stable data is the practical fit.

quiz.question: What does a shared data domain sacrifice?
options: A narrow bounded context and isolated schema changes
quiz.explanation: Shared tables retain fast joins and integrity but broaden change, security, and governance boundaries.

exercise.title: Select an access pattern
exercise.prompt: For one cross-domain read, quantify payload size, update rate, latency target, instance count, availability need, and consistency promise, then select and defend one access pattern.

fields.label: Context
fields.placeholder: Owner, consumer, data shape, and workload

fields.label: Decision
fields.placeholder: Chosen pattern and contract or sync rule

fields.label: Trade-off
fields.placeholder: Freshness, memory, latency, failure, and governance cost

steps.text: State who writes the fact and what freshness and access contract the owner can guarantee.
Compare call, column copy, replicated cache, and shared domain against volume and volatility.
If data is copied, define ownership, synchronization, startup, memory, and lag behavior.
Verify consumer latency and outage behavior with fitness measurements before widening the boundary.
